I will keep my farm centered on the Quzhou pattern that I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize, with a smaller block of spring peanut. I know this land, I know the machinery rhythm, and I care about stable grain first. Quzhou is a plain grain county, wheat and maize already fit the local heat, harvest windows, and mechanized operations very well. I would not chase too many scattered crops at my age, even with high education, because complexity creates timing mistakes. I would keep most of the land in the familiar double-cropping system and reserve a smaller share for peanut to lower water pressure, spread market risk, and give part of the land a different nutrient demand.

For wheat, I will use improved seed and manage it more carefully than traditionally, but I will not overfeed nitrogen. I want solid tillering, strong stems, and reliable grain filling rather than lush, wasteful growth. I will irrigate three times in a normal year: once around overwintering recovery, once at jointing, and once near grain filling if moisture is short. I will control weeds and major diseases with a limited number of pesticide passes instead of spraying blindly. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize with no-tillage seeding on most of that ground so I save time and moisture. I will use a hybrid maize because I want stand uniformity and higher yield potential. On the peanut field, I will keep fertilizer moderate, emphasize phosphorus and potassium more than nitrogen, irrigate only when needed, and use it as my lower-water, lower-input block for the year.
